explanation: A suppression rule hides matching alerts going forward but doesn't delete past alerts or change what Defender for Cloud already recorded. To see the alerts generated on those 10 VMs during the last five days, you adjust the filter and time range on the Security alerts page so the suppressed alerts are shown again. Changing the rule's expiration date (A) or disabling the rule (B) only affects future alert suppression, not the retrieval of already-suppressed alerts from the past. Reviewing local Windows event logs (D) does not give you Defender for Cloud's correlated, classified security alerts.

This is a hotspot question whose exact pixel-level selections can't be verified from the scraped data, so the originally recorded selection is kept as-is. Conceptually, a Defender for Cloud suppression rule is scoped using an entity type (such as Resource ID, IP address, or Login) and a matching field value for that entity; to silence alerts tied specifically to one storage account during development, the entity type would be the resource identifier and the field would hold that storage account's resource ID, so only alerts for that resource are hidden rather than alerts tenant-wide. This lets teams suppress known, expected noise from a specific resource without disabling detection elsewhere.

Microsoft Sentinel automation rules natively support actions such as assigning an incident owner, changing its status/severity, and adding tags or a comment, all performed directly by the rule without any external call. Querying a threat-intelligence API, running a forensic script, or collecting a memory image are response actions that require invoking a playbook (Logic App) or Defender for Endpoint, not something an automation rule does on its own. Because the SOC wants the ownership and status set before any external workflow runs, these two actions belong in the automation rule itself, with any playbook invocation added afterward.

A Microsoft Sentinel playbook is an Azure Logic Apps workflow triggered by an automation rule that can call out to external systems, such as opening a ticket in a service-management platform and posting a message to a Teams or Slack channel, which matches Microsoft's documented 'bi-directional sync' and 'orchestration' playbook use cases. A workbook only visualizes data, a hunting query only searches data, and a Defender XDR device group is just a grouping construct for applying policies to devices, none of which can call external APIs or post to chat platforms.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint lets administrators assign an automation level per device group, ranging from full automatic remediation to levels that require security-team approval before any remediation action runs, which directly satisfies having standard devices remediate automatically while a sensitive server group waits for approval. Workbooks and hunting queries are for visualization and querying, not remediation control, and Purview audit-retention policies govern log retention, not endpoint remediation behavior.

The Windows Security Events via AMA connector relies on data collection rules (DCRs) to define exactly which event logs (All Security Events, Common, Minimal, or a Custom XPath-filtered set) are collected from each agent and which workspace/table they are sent to. A workbook only visualizes already-ingested data, a device isolation policy is a Defender for Endpoint containment action, and a threat analytics report summarizes threat intelligence, none of which control log collection scope or destination.

Near-real-time (NRT) analytics rules in Microsoft Sentinel are a special rule type hard-coded to run about once per minute with roughly a two-minute end-to-end delay, far lower than the built-in five-minute delay of standard scheduled rules, making them the right choice when even a one-minute detection delay matters. A scheduled rule with a daily interval introduces far more latency, and workbooks or manually run hunting queries are not automated detection mechanisms at all.

In Microsoft Defender XDR, turning a validated Advanced Hunting KQL query into a custom detection rule lets it run automatically on a schedule (every 1, 3, 12, or 24 hours), generate alerts when it matches, and optionally trigger response actions, exactly as described. A device inventory filter only narrows a device list view, a Sentinel workbook only visualizes data, and a Purview eDiscovery case is for legal content search, none of which run scheduled detection logic or produce alerts.

In the Microsoft Sentinel data lake, a KQL job is the specific feature for running a one-time or recurring scheduled KQL query against data lake tier data and promoting matching results into the analytics tier for faster, interactive use. A workbook only visualizes existing analytics-tier data, a Defender XDR device group is a policy-scoping construct, and a Purview audit search queries the unified audit log, none of which move data between Sentinel's lake and analytics tiers.

The Windows Forwarded Events (WEF) connector writes collected events to the WindowsEvent table rather than SecurityEvent, so built-in analytics rules written against SecurityEvent simply never see that data even though forwarding itself is healthy. This is a known table-mismatch gotcha; events from the Windows Security Events via AMA connector, by contrast, land in SecurityEvent. The other options are incorrect: forwarding doesn't suppress events, WEF data isn't limited to Defender XDR incidents, and SecurityEvent isn't Linux-only — it simply isn't populated by the WEF connector.

The Defender for Endpoint device timeline (on the device page) provides exactly the chronological view of observed events, associated alerts, process-tree relationships, and MITRE ATT&CK technique tags for a single device, making it the natural first stop for a per-endpoint behavioral investigation. The vulnerability recommendation list and workbook gallery don't show event-level activity, and the email entity page is for message-centric, not device-centric, investigation.

Live response gives analysts an instantaneous remote shell connection to a device so they can run investigative commands, collect forensic artifacts, and take remediation actions in real time, without needing an interactive logged-on user session. Threat analytics is a reporting feature about threat campaigns, Purview Audit tracks M365 admin/user activity rather than live device interaction, and a Sentinel workbook only visualizes data, so none of them provide direct remote command execution on an endpoint.

The 'Collect investigation package' response action on a device page bundles forensic data about the device's current state (such as running processes, autoruns, and other artifacts) into a downloadable zipped folder analysts can examine outside the live portal session. Restrict app execution and automated attack disruption are containment actions, not evidence-collection packages, and a Sentinel hunting bookmark only saves query results rather than capturing device-state forensics.

Microsoft Purview Audit records who performed an action and when across Microsoft 365 services, including administrative configuration changes, making it the right starting point for a 'who changed what setting, and when' question. eDiscovery content search is built to find message and file content, not admin activity logs; a Sentinel notebook is for data science/analysis workflows; and Defender for Endpoint live response investigates endpoints, not M365 tenant administrative changes.

eDiscovery content search is purpose-built to locate email, documents, and chat content across Exchange Online mailboxes, OneDrive accounts, and SharePoint sites using keyword queries and Boolean search conditions, which is exactly what's needed to find a distinctive phishing campaign phrase across those locations. Audit activity search surfaces administrative/user actions rather than message content, the device timeline is endpoint-focused, and Sentinel NRT analytics detect telemetry events rather than search message/document content.

Microsoft Defender for Identity monitors on-premises Active Directory signals and has a dedicated 'Suspected identity theft (pass-the-ticket)' detection (mapped to MITRE T1550.003) for exactly this lateral-movement technique, where a stolen Kerberos ticket is reused on a different computer. Defender for Cloud Apps focuses on SaaS/cloud app activity, Defender for Office 365 focuses on email/collaboration threats, and Purview eDiscovery is a content-search tool, none of which provide on-prem AD identity-based lateral movement detection.

Microsoft Defender XDR's automatic attack disruption directly contains the compromised endpoint (isolating/blocking most of its network traffic) and disables the compromised user account to prevent further sign-in, cutting off the two attacker footholds in real time while remaining reversible by the security team. Collecting an investigation package is evidence gathering rather than disruption, exporting an incident to a workbook is visualization, and searching Purview Audit is investigative lookup, so none of those three directly interrupt an active attack the way containment and account disablement do.

The DeviceProcessEvents table in the Defender XDR Advanced Hunting schema specifically stores process creation and related process events reported by onboarded devices, making it the correct starting table for process-focused hunting. DeviceNetworkEvents covers network connections, DeviceFileEvents covers file system activity, and DeviceRegistryEvents covers registry modifications, none of which are the primary source for process creation telemetry.
